```{r}

    read_metrics() -> metrics_infos

  epsg_rast %>%

  list.files(paste0(wd, "/analysis/imputation"), pattern = paste0("results_", param$forest), full.names = T) %>%

    }) -> imputation_results
  
  imputation_results %>% 
    pull(knn_vars) %>% 
    str_remove(",X,Y") %>% 
    strsplit(",") %>% 
    unlist() %>% 
    unique() -> imputation_metrics
  
  readRDS(paste0(wd, "/analysis/segmentation/best_parameters_all.rds")) %>% 
    filter(forest == param$forest,
           model_name == names(param$models),
           type == "by_forest_model") -> segmentation_parameters
  
  segmentation_wd <- paste0(wd, "/segmentation/", param$forest, "/", names(param$models))
  # dir.create(segmentation_wd)
  
  # Catalog
  st_read(paste0(wd, "/shapefiles/", param$forest, "/ctg.shp"), quiet = T) %>%
    st_transform(epsg) -> ctg
  
  # Metrics
  metrics_infos %>%
    filter(name %in% c(segmentation_metrics,
                       imputation_metrics,
                       summary_metrics)) -> metrics_infos_selected
  
  metrics_infos_selected %>%
    pull(name) -> metrics_names
  
  metrics_infos_selected %>%
    pull(path) %>%
    map(rast) %>%
    map(project, epsg_rast, method = "bilinear") %>%
    map(resample, epsg_rast) %>%
    rast -> metrics
  
  names(metrics) <- metrics_names # Assign metrics names
  
  # # Masks
  # list(vect(paste0(wd, "/shapefiles/", param$forest, "/roads.shp")),
  #      vect(paste0(wd, "/shapefiles/", param$forest, "/waterbodies.shp"))) %>%
  #   map(project, epsg_rast) -> masks
  
  # Photo-interpreted polygons (fri)
  st_read(paste0(wd, "/shapefiles/", param$forest, "/PolygonForest.shp"), quiet = T) %>%
    rowid_to_column("id") %>%
    st_transform(epsg) -> fri_polygons
  
  # Landcover
  rast(paste0(wd, "/metrics/", param$forest, "/other/landcover.tif")) %>%
    terra::project(epsg_rast, method = "near") -> landcover
  
  landcover_codes <- c(`1` = "Clear_Open_Water",
                       `2` = "Turbid_Water",
                       `3` = "Shoreline",
                       `4` = "Mudflats",
                       `5` = "Marsh",
                       `6` = "Swamp",
                       `7` = "Fen",
                       `8` = "Bog",
                       `10` = "Heath",
                       `11` = "Sparse_Treed",
                       `12` = "Treed_Upland",
                       `13` = "Deciduous_Treed",
                       `14` = "Mixed_Treed",
                       `15` = "Coniferous_Treed",
                       `16` = "Plantations_Treed_Cultivated",
                       `17` = "Hedge_Rows",
                       `18` = "Disturbance",
                       `19` = "Open_Cliff_Talus",
                       `20` = "Alvar",
                       `21` = "Sand_Barren_Dune",
                       `22` = "Open_Tallgrass_Prairie",
                       `23` = "Tallgrass_Savannah",
                       `24` = "Tallgrass_Woodland",
                       `25` = "Sand_Gravel_Mine_Tailings_Extraction",
                       `26` = "Bedrock",
                       `27` = "Communit_Infrastructure",
                       `28` = "Agriculture_Undifferentiated_Rural_Land_Use",
                       `157` = "Other",
                       `247` = "Cloud_Shadow")
  
  # Attach levels (lookup table)
  levels(landcover) <- data.frame(value = as.integer(names(landcover_codes)),
                                  class = unname(landcover_codes))
  
  # Forest age in 2019
  rast(paste0(wd, "/metrics/", param$forest, "/other/forest_age_2019.tif")) %>%
    terra::project(epsg_rast, method = "near") -> forest_age_2019
  
  # Forest fire between 1985-2020
  rast(paste0(wd, "/metrics/", param$forest, "/other/forest_fire_1985_2020.tif")) %>%
    terra::project(epsg_rast, method = "near") -> forest_fire_1985_2020
  
  # Forest harvest between 1985-2020
  rast(paste0(wd, "/metrics/", param$forest, "/other/forest_harvest_1985_2020.tif")) %>%
    terra::project(epsg_rast, method = "near") -> forest_harvest_1985_2020
  
  # Segmentation
  eFRI_segmentation(metrics = metrics[[segmentation_metrics]],
                    # masks = masks,
                    masks = NULL,
                    thresh = segmentation_parameters$thresh,
                    spec = segmentation_parameters$spec,
                    spat = segmentation_parameters$spat,
                    method = "bs",
                    clean_nodata = TRUE,
                    ofile = paste0(segmentation_wd, "/", names(param$models), ".tif"),
                    otb_dir = otb_dir) -> segmentation

  segmentation %>%
    st_write(paste0(segmentation_wd, "/data.gpkg"),
             layer = names(param$models),
             quiet = T)
  
  # eFRI attibute table
  eFRI_attribute_table(segmentation = segmentation,
                       metrics = metrics,
                       summary_metrics = summary_metrics,
                       landcover = landcover,
                       forest_fire = forest_fire_1985_2020,
                       forest_harvest = forest_harvest_1985_2020,
                       forest_age = forest_age_2019) -> segmentation_data 
  
  segmentation_data %>% 
    dplyr::select(-id_seg, -id) %>% 
    rename(HEIGHT = Z_P95,
           CANOPY_COVER = Z_ABOVE2,
           MOISTURE = SAGAWI) -> segmentation_data
  
  segmentation_data %>% 
    st_write(paste0(segmentation_wd, "/data.gpkg"), 
             layer = paste0(names(param$models), "_data"),
             quiet = T)
  
  # Imputation
  eFRI_imputation(segmentation = segmentation_data,
                  forest_polygon = fri_polygons,
                  metrics = metrics,
                  landcover = landcover,
                  forest_fire = forest_fire_1985_2020,
                  forest_harvest = forest_harvest_1985_2020,
                  ctg = ctg,
                  lidar_year_column = "Fl_Cr_Y",
                  forest_year_column = "YRUPD",
                  forest_composition_column = "SPCOMP",
                  forest_type_column = "POLYTYPE",
                  target_variables = imputation_results$target_var,
                  knn_variables = imputation_results$knn_vars) -> segmentation_data_imputation
  
  segmentation_data_imputation %>% 
    st_write(paste0(segmentation_wd, "/data.gpkg"), 
             layer = paste0(names(param$models), "_data_imputation"),
             quiet = T)
  
  # Smooth polygons
  arcpy$SmoothPolygon_cartography(in_features = paste0(segmentation_wd, "/data.gpkg/", names(param$models), "_data_imputation"),
                                  out_feature_class = paste0(segmentation_wd, "/data.gpkg/", names(param$models), "_data_imputation_smoothed"),
                                  algorithm = "PAEK",
                                  tolerance = 100,
                                  endpoint_option = "FIXED_ENDPOINT",
                                  error_option = "RESOLVE_ERRORS")
}
```

# **1** Overview of the workflow {-#summary}

The workflow has three components, applied separately to each forest management unit (FMU) (@fig-workflow):

1. **Automated stand delineation** ([Section 2](#segmentation)). LiDAR metrics, and Sentinel-2 bands for comparison, are segmented into stand polygons. Segmentation parameters are calibrated so that polygons resemble FRI polygons in size and shape.
2. **Polygon attribution** ([Section 3](#attribute-table)). Each polygon receives forest attributes, land cover, stand age and disturbance information from existing raster products, and species composition by imputation or from a species map.
3. **Performance assessment** ([Section 4](#performance-assessment)). Automated and FRI polygons are compared in validation areas against independent, high-resolution reference layers.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-workflow
%%| fig-cap: "Overview of the automated stand delineation, attribution and assessment workflow."
flowchart LR
  A["SPL LiDAR metrics (20 m)"] --> C["GRM segmentation"]
  B["Sentinel-2 bands (20 m)"] -.-> C
  M["Non-forest masks (water, roads)"] -.-> C
  P["FRI polygons"] -- "calibration of polygon size and shape" --> C
  C --> D["Smoothing"]
  D --> E["Polygon attribution"]
  F["EFI rasters, land cover, age, fire and harvest"] --> E
  G["Species composition (kNN or species map)"] --> E
  E --> H["Attributed stand layer"]
  D --> I["Performance assessment in validation areas"]
  R["Drone LiDAR and field plots (1 m reference layers)"] --> I
```

\newpage

# **2** Automated stand delineation {-#segmentation}

## **2.1** Input data {-#segmentation-data}

Stands were delineated from 20 m raster layers describing either forest structure (SPL LiDAR) or the spectral properties of the canopy (Sentinel-2). Several combinations of layers were tested to measure what each source contributes to stand delineation.

### **2.1.1** Single-photon LiDAR {-#segmentation-data-spl}

Both FMUs are covered by leaf-on single-photon LiDAR (SPL) acquired for Ontario's Forest Resources Inventory program. Over RMF, data were collected in June and July 2018 with a Leica SPL100 sensor (50% overlap between flight lines, about 41 points/m²). Over OVF, data were collected in **[TO COMPLETE: year, sensor, point density]**. Structural metrics describing canopy height, canopy cover and the vertical distribution of vegetation were computed on a 20 m grid from height-normalized point clouds, using the open-source R packages lidR and lasR (Roussel et al., 2020).

### **2.1.2** Sentinel-2 {-#segmentation-data-sentinel2}

A cloud-free growing-season composite (June 1 to August 31) was built from all available Sentinel-2A images acquired in the same year as the SPL data. All bands were resampled to 20 m and aligned on the SPL grid. Three bands were used: red edge (B6, about 740 nm), near infrared (B8) and shortwave infrared (B11). These bands are commonly used to distinguish forest types and species groups, notably broadleaf from coniferous canopies.

## **2.2** Segmentation algorithm {-#segmentation-algorithm}

Stands were delineated with the Generic Region Merging (GRM) tool of the open-source Orfeo ToolBox, using the Baatz & Schäpe criterion. This is the same principle as the multiresolution segmentation of the commercial software eCognition. The algorithm starts from individual pixels and merges neighbouring regions step by step, as long as the merged region remains sufficiently homogeneous. Homogeneity is assessed on the values of the input layers, such as LiDAR height and cover.

Three parameters control the result:

- **Threshold (scale):** the maximum heterogeneity allowed when two regions merge. A small threshold produces many small polygons; a large threshold produces fewer, larger polygons.
- **Spectral weight:** the importance given to similarity of input values. A high weight makes boundaries closely follow changes in the input layers.
- **Spatial weight:** the importance given to compact, smooth shapes. A high weight produces more regular polygons, at the cost of some internal homogeneity.

A short [video by Trimble](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tt53hoRAw9Q) explains how these parameters interact in eCognition.

## **2.3** Calibration of segmentation parameters {-#Segmentation-parameter-optimization}

GRM parameters have no direct forestry meaning. They were therefore calibrated so that automated polygons resemble FRI polygons in density, size and shape. For each FMU and each combination of input layers, 1,000 parameter combinations were tested in 5 × 5 km calibration areas **[TO CONFIRM: ten areas in each FMU?]**. Combinations that changed polygon density by more than about 10% relative to the FRI were discarded. Among the others, the combination whose distributions of polygon area and shape best overlapped those of FRI polygons was retained.

This calibration keeps automated stands operationally plausible. It uses only the FRI polygons, not the reference data later used to assess stand quality. The procedure is detailed in [Appendix A](segmentation_parameters_optimisation.qmd).

## **2.4** Delineation scenarios and FMU-wide delineations {-#Segmentation-generation}

Three delineation scenarios were compared (@tbl-scenarios). They test whether structural information (SPL), spectral information (Sentinel-2), or both, give the best stands. A fourth scenario, combining SPL metrics with a topographic wetness index, was also tested and is reported in the scientific article **[TO COMPLETE: reference once available]**.

| Scenario | Input layers | Information captured |
|---|---|---|
| SPL only | z_p95, z_above2, z_skew | Canopy height, canopy cover and vertical structure |
| SPL + S2 red edge | z_p95, z_above2, Sentinel-2 B6 | Height and cover, plus a spectral signal related to composition |
| S2 only | Sentinel-2 B6, B8, B11 | Spectral properties of the canopy only |

: Delineation scenarios compared in the project. {#tbl-scenarios}

Each scenario was run with its calibrated parameters over the full extent of each FMU. The "SPL only" scenario was retained to produce the final attributed layers, because it performed consistently well in both FMUs and relies only on provincial SPL data (see [Results](project_outputs.qmd#performance-assessment)). Its three input metrics are shown in @fig-segmentation-data-1 to @fig-segmentation-data-3:

- **z_p95:** 95th percentile of return heights above 1.3 m, a measure of dominant canopy height;
- **z_above2:** proportion of first returns above 2 m, a measure of canopy cover;
- **z_skew:** skewness of return heights above 1.3 m, which indicates whether vegetation is concentrated near the top of the canopy or in lower layers.

These three metrics are one possible choice. Any raster describing forest conditions can be used as segmentation input, and the chosen layers determine where boundaries are drawn. Adding a terrain moisture index, for example, tends to separate stands growing on contrasting site conditions. Inputs should carry complementary information; a correlation matrix or a principal component analysis helps avoid redundant layers.

# **3** Polygon attribution {-#attribute-table}

Each polygon was attributed in two ways: by direct extraction from existing raster products, and by imputation for attributes that no raster describes.

## **3.1** Input data {-#attribute-table-data}

@tbl-attribute-sources lists the layers used, which are shown for RMF in @fig-eFRI-attibute-table-data-1 to @fig-eFRI-attibute-table-data-8.

| Layer | Source | Resolution | Period |
|---|---|---|---|
| Land cover | Ontario Land Cover Compilation v2.0 | **[TO COMPLETE]** | Imagery 1999–2011 |
| Forest age | NTEMS forest age (Maltman et al., 2023) | 30 m | 2019 |
| Fire and harvest | NTEMS disturbance maps (Hermosilla et al., 2016) | 30 m | 1985–2020 |
| Volume, QMDBH, stem density, basal area | **[TO COMPLETE: source of EFI rasters]** | 20 m | **[TO COMPLETE]** |
| Height, canopy cover | SPL metrics (z_p95, z_above2) | 20 m | 2018 (RMF) |
| Slope, soil moisture | **[TO COMPLETE: DEM source]**, SAGA wetness index | **[TO COMPLETE]** | — |

: Raster layers used to attribute the polygons. {#tbl-attribute-sources}

**Land cover.** The [Ontario Land Cover Compilation v2.0](https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=7aa998fdf100434da27a41f1c637382c) merges provincial land cover products into 27 classes, derived from Landsat imagery acquired between 1999 and 2011. It was used to estimate the forested proportion and the dominant land cover of each polygon.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eFRI-attibute-table-data-1
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Land cover from the Ontario Land Cover Compilation v2.0."
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data = sat_forest*1.5) +
  geom_spatraster(data = landcover) +
  scale_fill_discrete(na.translate = FALSE) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(fill = "Landcover type") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Forest age.** The forest age map of the National Terrestrial Ecosystem Monitoring System ([NTEMS](https://opendata.nfis.org/mapserver/nfis-change_eng.html)) gives stand age in 2019 at 30 m resolution across Canada ([Maltman et al., 2023](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425723000809)). Age is derived directly from mapped disturbances where available, from spectral recovery after disturbance where the disturbance date is inferred, and otherwise from height and growth models (86.6% of the forested area). Stands older than 150 years are grouped in a single class.

```{r}
#| label: fig-eFRI-attibute-table-data-2
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Forest age in 2019 from the National Terrestrial Ecosystem Monitoring System (NTEMS)."
ggplot() +
  geom_spatraster_rgb(data = sat_forest*1.5) +
  geom_spatraster(data = forest_age_2019) +
  scale_fill_whitebox_c(palette = "muted",
                        breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(n = 3)) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = c(0, 0)) +
  theme_bw() +
  labs(fill = "Forest age in 2019") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

**Fire and harvest.** The NTEMS disturbance maps give, for each 30 m pixel, the year of the main stand-replacing fire or harvest between 1985 and 2020, detected automatically from Landsat time series ([Hermosilla et al., 2016](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/17538947.2016.1187673)).

```{r}
#| label: fig-eFRI-attibute-table-data-3
#| echo: false
#| results: hide
```

## **3.2** Attributes extracted for each polygon {-#attribute-table-assignment}

@tbl-attributes lists the attributes assigned to each automated polygon. Field names follow FRI conventions where possible. This table also serves as the data dictionary of the final layers.

| Field | Description | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| SOURCE | Data source ("eFRI") | — |
| YRSOURCE | Year the polygon layer was produced (2026) | year |
| AREA | Polygon area | m² |
| PERIMETER | Polygon perimeter | m |
| PROPFORESTED | Share of the polygon in forested land cover classes^1^ | % |
| POLYTYPE | Most frequent land cover class | class |
| POLYTYPEPROP | Share of the polygon in the most frequent land cover class | % |
| AGE | Mean stand age in YRSOURCE, from the NTEMS age map | years |
| YRDEP | Year of the last disturbance affecting at least 80% of the polygon | year |
| DEPTYPE | Type of the last disturbance (FIRE or HARVEST) | class |
| DEPPROP | Share of the polygon affected by the last disturbance | % |
| YRHARVEST | Year of the harvest covering the largest share of the polygon | year |
| HARVESTPROP | Share of the polygon covered by that harvest | % |
| YRFIRE | Year of the fire covering the largest share of the polygon | year |
| FIREPROP | Share of the polygon covered by that fire | % |
| VMERCH_HA | Merchantable volume | m³/ha |
| QMDBH | Quadratic mean diameter at breast height | cm |
| DENS | Stem density, trees with DBH > 7.1 cm **[TO CONFIRM]** | stems/ha |
| BA_HA | Basal area | m²/ha |
| HEIGHT | Stand height, median of z_p95 | m |
| CANOPY_COVER | Canopy cover, median of z_above2 | % |
| SLOPE | Median slope | % |
| MOISTURE | Soil moisture, SAGA wetness index | index |

## **3.3** Imputation of species composition {-#imputation}

No raster currently describes species composition across Ontario. Species attributes were therefore estimated by [k-nearest neighbour (kNN) imputation](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0034425721001954): each new polygon receives the attribute values of the most similar FRI polygons, similarity being measured on LiDAR metrics and on location (polygon centroid coordinates). Categorical attributes, such as the leading species, take the most frequent value among neighbours; numeric attributes take their mean.

The imputation was set up separately for each FMU and each imputed attribute:

1. **Reference polygons.** FRI polygons affected by a fire or harvest between photo-interpretation and the SPL acquisition were removed, since their FRI description no longer matched the LiDAR data. Only forested polygons were kept: POLYTYPE equal to FOR, more than 50% forested land cover, z_p95 of at least 5 m and z_above2 of at least 0.5.
2. **Candidate metrics.** Correlated LiDAR metrics were grouped (correlation threshold of 0.8). In each group, the metric most strongly related to the imputed attribute (highest one-way ANOVA F-value) was kept.
3. **Selection of the best combination.** All combinations of five candidate metrics (7,865 or 9,633 combinations, depending on the attribute) were tested, each together with the centroid coordinates. The combination that best reproduced the FRI values was retained.

Imputation accuracy is reported in [Results](project_outputs.qmd#attribute-table-results-imputation).

# **4** Performance assessment {-#performance-assessment}

The automated delineations were compared with the FRI polygons using three questions that a forest manager might ask of any stand map:

1. **Internal homogeneity:** are stands internally uniform?
2. **Partitioning of variability:** do stands separate areas that differ in structure?
3. **Boundary correspondence:** are boundaries drawn where forest structure actually changes?

Answering these questions requires reference data that are independent of both the FRI and the SPL data used for segmentation. Reference layers were therefore produced from drone LiDAR and field plots in four 50-ha validation areas per FMU (see the [study area map](index.qmd#introduction-study-area)), and all assessments were carried out within these areas.

## **4.1** Validation areas and field data {-#methods-validation-areas}

Validation areas were selected to include several stands and boundaries typical of each FMU, in locations accessible for field work. In OVF, they cover tolerant hardwood and hemlock stands managed by selection, white pine and oak shelterwoods, and mixed and intolerant hardwood clearcuts. In RMF, they cover jack pine and spruce–pine uplands, black spruce–cedar–larch lowlands, poplar and white birch hardwoods, and mixedwoods.

A total of 61 circular field plots of 400 m² were measured (30 in RMF, 31 in OVF). Plot locations were chosen with a structurally guided sampling design (sgsR package; Goodbody et al., 2023), so that plots covered the range of canopy structures present while avoiding roads, water and stand edges. In each plot, species, diameter at breast height (DBH) and health status were recorded for all live trees with a DBH of at least 9.1 cm, and plot centres were positioned with a survey-grade GNSS receiver. Basal area, merchantable volume, quadratic mean diameter and stem density were then computed for each plot.

Each validation area was also scanned by drone LiDAR (DJI Matrice 300 RTK with a Zenmuse L2 sensor), producing point clouds of about 540 points/m², more than ten times denser than the SPL data.

## **4.2** Reference forest attribute layers {-#methods-reference-forest-attribute}

Reference layers were produced with the area-based approach commonly used in enhanced forest inventories (White et al., 2013). Plot attributes were related to drone LiDAR metrics computed over the same 400 m² footprint, using random forest models (Breiman, 2001). Separate models were fitted for each FMU **[TO CONFIRM: by FMU or by validation area]** and each attribute: merchantable volume, quadratic mean diameter (QMDBH) and stem density. Predictors were selected by grouping correlated metrics and then iteratively removing the least important ones, keeping the model with the lowest cross-validated error (5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times). The final models explained 54% to 75% of the variation in plot attributes, with negligible bias. Canopy height, the fourth reference attribute, was taken directly from the drone LiDAR as the 90th percentile of return heights (z_p90).

The models were then applied wall-to-wall. Drone LiDAR metrics were computed for each 1 m pixel over the surrounding 20 × 20 m window, so that predictions keep the 400 m² support of the field plots while giving very detailed maps (Roussel et al., 2020). The result is a set of 1 m reference layers, independent of the FRI and of the SPL data, against which every delineation was assessed.

## **4.3** Partitioning of forest attribute variability {-#partitioning-forest-attribute-variability}

The proportion of variance explained (PVE) measures how much of the variation of a reference attribute within a validation area is explained by differences between polygons:

$$
PVE = 1 - \frac{SS_{\text{within}}}{SS_{\text{total}}}
$$

where SS~within~ is the sum of squared differences between each pixel and the mean of its polygon, and SS~total~ is the sum of squared differences between each pixel and the mean of the validation area. PVE ranges from 0 to 1. A high value means that polygons separate areas with different structure, so that most of the variation occurs between polygons rather than within them.

## **4.4** Internal polygon homogeneity {-#internal-polygon-homogeneity}

Internal homogeneity was measured by the area-weighted mean of within-polygon standard deviations (wSD):

$$
wSD = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i \times SD_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i}
$$

where a~i~ is the area of polygon *i* within the validation area and SD~i~ is the standard deviation of the reference attribute within that polygon. Only polygons with at least 1 ha inside the validation area were included, and values were averaged over the four validation areas of each FMU. A lower wSD means more uniform stands.

## **4.5** Correspondence of stand boundaries with structural transitions {-#correspondence-structural-transition}

Boundary correspondence was assessed by first detecting structural transitions directly in the reference layers, then checking whether stand boundaries fall at these transitions. The analysis was run separately for each reference attribute, using a split moving window (SMW) approach:

1. **Transects.** In each validation area, a grid of 72 transects (36 north–south and 36 east–west, about 20 m apart) was laid over the reference layers. Along each transect, attribute values were averaged over 10 m on each side of the line, which smooths out very local features such as a single canopy gap.
2. **Detection of transitions.** A 20 m window was moved along each transect, one metre at a time. At each position, the mean attribute value over the 10 m before the position was compared with the mean over the 10 m after it. Positions where this difference was exceptionally large, above the 95th percentile of all values in the FMU, were flagged as structural transitions, keeping only the strongest transition within any 40 m stretch.
3. **Matching with stand boundaries.** Each point where a transect crosses a stand boundary was matched with the nearest detected transition within 20 m, which corresponds to the pixel size of the segmentation inputs. Each transition could be matched with only one boundary crossing, and vice versa.

Agreement was then summarized by three statistics for each FMU, attribute and delineation:

- **Precision:** the proportion of stand boundaries located at a detected transition;
- **Recall:** the proportion of detected transitions captured by a stand boundary;
- **F1-score:** the harmonic mean of precision and recall, which balances the two.

$$
F_1 = \frac{2 \times \text{Precision} \times \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}
$$

Results are expressed as the percentage change in F1-score of each automated delineation relative to the FRI, for the same attribute. A sensitivity analysis varied the window size (10 to 40 m **[TO CONFIRM]**), the lateral averaging (none, 5 m or 10 m on each side) and the matching tolerance (5, 10 or 20 m). These settings changed the size of the differences between delineations, but not their ranking.
